analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from collecting or selling people's reproductive and sexual health data except to provide a service they asked for.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 119 House cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped companies from collecting, keeping, using, or selling personal reproductive and sexual health information unless it was strictly needed to provide a product or service the person actually requested. It would have given people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, required plain-language privacy policies, and let people sue violators in court, with the Federal Trade Commission also able to enforce it. It was introduced after the Supreme Court returned abortion regulation to the states, when records like period-tracker entries, location data near clinics, and search histories can be bought by data brokers and potentially used to investigate or prosecute people.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses apps or websites that touch reproductive or sexual health data — period trackers, fertility apps, pharmacy and clinic websites, search and maps. The bill would have limited what companies can keep and sell about them, given them access, correction, and deletion rights at no fee, barred companies from punishing them for using those rights, and let them sue with statutory damages of at least $100 per violation per day. It also barred pre-dispute arbitration clauses for these claims, meaning companies could not force people into private arbitration instead of court. People in states where abortion is restricted stood to benefit the most, because data trails could otherwise expose them to investigation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health and period-tracking apps

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits regulated entities from collecting, retaining, using, or disclosing personal reproductive or sexual health information except as strictly necessary to provide a product or service the individual requested, and restricts employee access to that data [S2].

Gives individuals the right to access their data (including how it was collected and which third parties received it), correct it, and have it deleted, with companies required to respond within 15 days and barred from charging fees [S2].
Requires a clear, prominently published privacy policy naming the specific third parties a company shares reproductive health data with and why [S2].
Bars companies from retaliating against people who exercise these rights, such as by denying service or changing prices [S2].

Lets individuals sue violators for $100–$1,000 per violation per day plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, treats a violation as a concrete injury for standing purposes, and makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for these disputes; the FTC can also enforce the Act [S2].

Covers inferred and algorithmically derived data — for example, conclusions about pregnancy or sexual activity drawn from non-health data — and location data that might indicate seeking reproductive care [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that collect, use, broker, or advertise against reproductive and sexual health data: period and fertility apps, data brokers, ad-tech firms, and platforms. They would face compliance costs, lose access to a data category they currently sell, and face litigation exposure including statutory damages. The bill excluded HIPAA-covered doctors, hospitals, and their business associates, so ordinary medical privacy rules would not have changed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers, ad-tech, and health apps

drawbacks.text: The definition of regulated data is broad — including inferred information and anything tied to menstruation, pregnancy, or sexual activity — so compliance costs could fall heavily on small app developers, not just large data brokers [S2].

The private right of action with statutory damages of $100–$1,000 per violation per day could generate substantial litigation against companies even for technical violations, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2].

The bill leaves state privacy laws in place rather than creating one uniform national standard, which companies argue means following a patchwork of rules; it also preserves stronger state protections [S2].
Entities covered by HIPAA are excluded, so the bill would not have strengthened privacy protections at doctors' offices, hospitals, and clinics — only at the apps and websites outside HIPAA [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: in a country where abortion is legal in some states and restricted in others, commercial data trails — a missed period logged in an app, a GPS ping near a clinic, a search for medication abortion — can be bought and resold, and the bill would have sharply limited that market while giving people direct control over their own data. The costs are real but ordinary for a privacy law: compliance burdens, litigation risk, and a state-law patchwork. The main design gap is the HIPAA exclusion, which leaves the formal medical system untouched and targets the commercial data economy instead — which is precisely where most people's data is least protected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on May 17, 2023 by Rep. Sara Jacobs with 89 original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on May 19, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 118th Congress [S4].
It ended the Congress with 119 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, ad-tech firms, and app makers that collect and monetize reproductive and sexual health data are better off, since they faced no new restrictions, and they never even had to fight the bill on the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and health-data app makers

for.name: Rep. Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 119 Democratic cosponsors for it.

for.name: 119 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, so it stayed in committee without a vote.

against.name: House Republicans on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: As the chamber's majority party, took no action to advance the bill out of committee during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 119 cosponsors were House Democrats out of 216; the record lists no Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-majority committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: These firms buy, infer, and resell location and behavioral data that can reveal pregnancies, clinic visits, and contraceptive use. The bill would have barred collecting or disclosing such data except to serve a customer's actual request, cutting off a lucrative data category, which is why its interest runs against the public's privacy.

Apps would face new collection limits, deletion duties, and lawsuit exposure, but they would also have to disclose exactly who they sell users' data to, which could build trust with users whose trust is currently the product being sold.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and HIPAA-covered health systems
industries.note: They are excluded from the bill when acting under HIPAA privacy rules, so their legal obligations would not change; nothing in the bill adds to or subtracts from their compliance burden.
